sections.h2: Where does an Ohio County, Kentucky owner pay the tax bill?
sections.html:
Property tax is paid in the sheriff's tax office, 301 South Main Street in Hartford. Checks sent by mail use PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347, and the phone is 270-298-4444.

The county's sheriff page lists weekday counter hours of 8 a.m.-4 p.m. and a half day (8 a.m.-noon) on each month's first and last Saturday. A drop box is mounted on the door for after-hours payments. Postmarks are honored on mailed checks, and cash should never go in an envelope. A card works at the counter, and the sheriff's website has an online payment link. Refund checks, for example after a corrected assessment, are mailed at the end of each month, and the tax office takes refund questions on the same phone line.

Values are set elsewhere. An assessment, address or exemption question goes to the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) at 270-298-4433.

sections.h2: How large is Ohio County, and who lives there?
sections.html:
Ohio County is big and sparsely settled. Its 587 square miles of land rank fifth among Kentucky's 120 counties, yet the 2020 density was only about 40 people per square mile. Hartford holds the courthouse and Beaver Dam is the biggest town. Centertown, Fordsville, McHenry and Rockport round out the cities, with Rosine as a census-designated place. Rough River runs through the middle, and Green River traces the southwest edge.

The legislature carved the county out of Hardin County in 1798, and its coal mines made it well known across the region. In January 1865 Confederate cavalry burned the Hartford courthouse, although the county records had been carried out beforehand.

The head count tells its own story. Ohio County had 1,223 people in 1800, peaked at 27,642 in 1910 and fell to 17,725 by 1960 as farms and mines shed workers. It climbed back to 21,765 in 1980 and has hovered near 24,000 since 2010 (23,842 in the 2010 census and 23,772 in 2020, with density holding at roughly 40.5 people per square mile). Census Bureau figures sketch the housing picture.

  • Population: 23,934 by the July 2025 estimate, a 0.7 percent gain over April 2020.
  • Value of a typical owned house: $121,400 (2020 to 2024 survey), with $1,105 in monthly costs for those who carry a mortgage.
  • Ownership: 77.2 percent of the 9,107 households.
  • Income: $57,798 for the median household, with 15.3 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Age: 20.6 percent of residents are 65 or older.
  • Supply: 10,377 housing units and just 3 building permits in 2025.

sections.h2: What are the Ohio County payment periods and penalties?
sections.html:
Bills become payable on October 1. The sheriff publishes the calendar below, and the assessment date behind every bill is January 1.

Ohio County collection calendar (Ohio County Sheriff's Office, property tax information page)
DatesAmount due
October 1 to November 1Bill less 2 percent
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to 31Face amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Face amount plus 21 percent
After April 15Bill transfers to the County Clerk

KRS 134.015 lists a flat 10 percent for that stretch, so ask the tax office to price your parcel exactly.

If October 10 passes with no bill, the sheriff asks owners to call and will send a duplicate by mail, fax or email. A copy sent elsewhere is a one-time courtesy. The PVA alone changes the standing mailing address.

sections.h2: What happens to Ohio County bills left unpaid on April 15?
sections.html:
Prior-year payments stop at the sheriff on April 15 and move to the Ohio County Clerk, at 301 S Main St, Suite 201 in Hartford (weekdays 8 a.m.-4:30 p.m.; recording desk 270-298-4423). The clerk's delinquent tax page announced a tax sale for October 23, 2025, which has passed, so ask for the next date.

  • The bill turns into a recorded lien, with 1 percent monthly interest added, according to the state revenue department.
  • Large-scale bidders (over three certificates here, five statewide or $10,000 in total) register with the state first.
  • A listed house with a certificate needs a written payoff from the clerk, since the balance grows each month.

sections.h2: Where does an Ohio County owner turn to contest a value?
sections.html: Begin with the PVA at 270-298-4433, where a conference must happen while the spring inspection period is open. Bring comparable sales, repair estimates and photos. A failed conference leads to a form at the County Clerk, then a local three-person board, then the state Board of Tax Appeals. The PVA appeal guide spells out each deadline, including 30 days to reach the state board.

sections.h2: Which breaks reduce an Ohio County tax bill?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption is open to residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Per the sheriff's page, a 70 percent VA rating or a 100 percent Social Security disability finding can also qualify, and the PVA decides each claim. It takes a set dollar amount off the assessed value, revised on a two-year cycle, and the next owner starts a new application.

Working farmland is taxed on what the land earns from farming, not on market price, and that can matter a great deal where 76 percent of residents live in rural areas.

sections.h2: What does an Ohio County seller owe beyond the tax bill?
sections.html:
The seller carries the state transfer tax: 50 cents per $500 of declared value, rounded up (KRS 142.050). At the $121,400 county median that is 243 units and $121.50, due before the clerk accepts the deed.

  • Confirm with the sheriff who is paying this year's bill.
  • Ask the clerk about any recorded lien or certificate.
  • Put a tax-bill mailing address in the deed, as KRS 382.135 demands.

sections.h2: What do owners and renters pay in Ohio County?
sections.html:
Carrying costs are modest. Owners with no mortgage pay a median of $395 a month, and renters pay a median gross of $739. The average household has 2.58 people, and per capita income is $28,772.

The Census counts 10,377 housing units against 9,107 occupied households, so roughly 1,270 units are empty, seasonal or on the market. Self-employed owners are common as well: the county had 1,351 nonemployer businesses in 2024, against 371 employer establishments in 2023.

sections.h2: Which parts of Ohio County's economy affect home sales?
sections.html:
Retail, health care and transportation carry the local economy. Stores rang up $255.6 million in 2022, or $10,876 per resident, according to the Census. Health care and social assistance took in $111.7 million, transportation and warehousing $58.4 million, and lodging and restaurants $23.3 million.

Employers supplied 7,858 jobs in 2023, a 14.3 percent rise over 2022, and paid $265.2 million in wages. A one-way trip to work takes 28.1 minutes on average, and broadband reaches 85.1 percent of homes.

The people side matters to a buyer too. Nine in ten residents (91.8 percent) were in the same house a year earlier, so few homes turn over. Only 13.9 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and 874 residents are veterans. Few homes change hands in any single small town, which makes pricing a house in Fordsville, Rockport or McHenry harder than in Beaver Dam.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Ohio County property tax?
faqs.a: The sheriff's tax office in Hartford, at 301 South Main Street. Mail checks to PO Box 186, Hartford, KY 42347.

faqs.q: When does a penalty begin on an Ohio County property tax bill?
faqs.a: On January 1. A 5 percent penalty covers that month, and any payment made from November 2 through the end of December costs just the face amount.

faqs.q: Can a house with an unpaid tax bill still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Payoff comes out of the proceeds, using a figure from the sheriff before April 15 or from the County Clerk after it.

faqs.q: Whom do I call to question my Ohio County valuation?
faqs.a: The PVA, 270-298-4433. Values are outside the sheriff's authority.

faqs.q: What transfer tax would a seller pay at the Ohio County median price?
faqs.a: $121.50 on a $121,400 sale, which counts as 243 units of $500.
